summary:
Cauca department is assessed at the national legal floor that applies to a trans visitor in Colombia, since the sources on this record contain no Cauca-specific statute, ruling or incident. That floor is comparatively strong. Consensual same-sex relations have been legal since 1981; Congress passed a national ban on discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in 2011; the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016, with the country's first same-sex wedding taking place in Cali on 24 May 2016; and adoption by same-sex couples has been available since 2015.

Legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition, a basis recognised in Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 and carrying no surgical requirement. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Birth certificates offer the markers F, M, NB and T, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The enforcement picture is the opposite of that legal position. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, and CNN's follow-up video feature of 6 August 2025 documents that killings did not stop after the Sara Millerey case, with gangs linked to queer and transgender deaths. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, in April 2025; a 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands flailing in a creek before she drowned, and her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities.

The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025. He praised the government's legal reforms and its commitment to equality while concluding that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Trans-specific violence with armed-group sponsorship is documented in this record in departments other than Cauca. In Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through street flyers and WhatsApp naming "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots" as legitimate military targets; three armed men gave a trans woman and local election candidate one week to leave town, after which she hid for a week and fled at night, and a friend of another trans woman was killed. Tatiana Céspedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after receiving death threats from armed men. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Eight trans women were killed in Colombia between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and discrimination limits trans women in Caquetá mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Whether that armed-group pattern operates in Cauca with trans-specific effects is not resolved by the available sources, and nothing on this record ties it to Cauca's countryside. Protection machinery has nonetheless been asserted at national level: in July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern; and a Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system. Until Cauca-specific evidence exists, the visitor should expect the national pattern of high violence against trans people alongside strong formal legal protection.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's legal framework is among the most developed in Latin America, yet the gap between that framework and enforcement is described by the UN Independent Expert as severe. A visitor to Cauca therefore meets a jurisdiction where the formal position is protective and the observed position is violent, and where the record's documentation is concentrated in the national aggregate rather than in the department.

The comparison across armed-group-affected departments is the clearest contrast available. Caquetá and Guajira carry named, dated documentation of flyers, kill lists and forced displacement; Cauca carries none of that in these sources despite armed-group activity in its countryside. The absence may reflect documentation rather than absence of the pattern, and the record does not permit a stronger conclusion.

Economic marginalisation is a documented compounding factor. Discrimination reported in Caquetá confines trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and Tatiana Céspedes's forced relocations show that trans business owners in armed-group areas face death threats irrespective of their occupation.

Domestic legal change is ongoing rather than settled. A comprehensive trans law was still before the legislature in 2025, and the introduction of "trans" and "non-binary" markers on national identification documents in November 2025 postdates most of the violence data in the record, so implementation experience is not yet evidenced.
localsOnly:
Colombian law permits a change of the sex marker on state identity documents by signed declaration before a notary, with no judicial order, psychiatric assessment or surgical requirement. Birth certificates carry the markers F, M, NB and T, and national identity documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

The 2011 national discrimination statute covers sexual orientation and applies to encounters with police, officials and public services. Trans detainees benefit from a court ruling on their treatment while deprived of liberty, and the Special Jurisdiction for Peace's July 2023 finding recognises conflict-related violence against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities as gender persecution rather than ordinary homicide.

Resident trans women in armed-group-affected departments such as Caquetá report limited livelihood options, death threats and forced relocation, and the departmental pattern is not unique: kill lists posted in Guajira in March 2024 named individuals under an anti-LGBTI wording.
